system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Consensus number
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Herlihy's wait-free hierarchy, which classifies object types by the largest number of processes for which they solve wait-free consensus. Covers the FLP-style impossibility arguments for levels 1 and 2, level-∞ objects, Ruppert's n-discerning characterization of readable objects, and the limits of the classification (robustness, combining operations). Excludes the universal construction details.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C03-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: In the wait-free hierarchy, an asynchronous shared-memory object type T has consensus number n if, using objects of type T and atomic registers (all initialized to appropriate values), wait-free consensus (agreement, validity, wait-free termination) can be solved for n processes but not for n+1 processes.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0205-s06] The wait-free hierarchy hrm classiﬁes asynchronous shared-memory object types T by consensus number, where a type T has consensus number n if with objects of type T and atomic registers (all initialized to appropriate values1) it is possible to solve wait-free consensus (i.e., agreement, validity, wait-free termination) for n processes but not for n + 1 processes.
- CS-DIST-C03-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Every object type has consensus number at least 1, because 1-process consensus requires no interaction, and the consensus number can range up to $\infty$ for particularly powerful objects.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0205-s07] The consensus number of any type is at least 1, since 1-process consensus requires no interaction, and may range up to ∞for particularly powerful objects.
- CS-DIST-C03-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: In the $h^r_m$ formulation of the hierarchy, an object type is at level n if unboundedly many objects of that type plus unboundedly many registers solve n-process wait-free consensus but not (n+1)-process wait-free consensus.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0206-s14] Various subsequent authors noticed that Herlihy’s slightly informal deﬁnition of consensus number did not give a robust hierarchy in the sense that combining two types of objects with consensus number n could solve wait-free consensus for larger n, and the hierarchy hrm was proposed by Jayanti [Jay97] as a way of classifying objects that might be robust: an object is at level n of the hrm hierarchy if having unboundedly many objects plus unboundedly many registers solves n-process wait-free consensus but not (n + 1)-process
    [CS-DIST-p0207-s01] CHAPTER 19.
    [CS-DIST-p0207-s02] THE WAIT-FREE HIERARCHY 175
    [CS-DIST-p0207-s03] wait-free consensus.2 There is some ﬂexibility in what assumptions we make about initialization and what version of consensus we solve.
- CS-DIST-C03-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: A readable object type T is n-discerning if there exist a reachable state $q_0$, a split of processes $p_1,\dots,p_n$ into two nonempty teams $A_0$ and $A_1$, and operations $\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n$ such that $R_{A_0,j}\cap R_{A_1,j}=\emptyset$ for all j, i.e., after any sequence of these operations each process can tell which team performed the first operation; for readable objects $h^r_m(T)\ge n$ if and only if T is n-discerning.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0221-s04] A readable object type T is n-discerning if it has a reachable state q0 in which it is possible to split processes p1, . . . , pn into two nonempty teams A0 and A1 and assign each process pi an operation πi, so that after any sequence of operations πi1, . . . , πik, each process can tell if the ﬁrst operation πi1 was performed by a process in team A0 or team A1.11 To formalize this, let us deﬁne RAb,j for each b ∈{0, 1} and each process id j as the set of all pairs ⟨r, q⟩for which there is an execution q0πi1, . . . , πik where (a) all the iℓare distinct; (b) one of them is pj, (c) pi1 ∈Ab, (d) pj’s operation returns r, and (e) the ﬁnal state of the object is q.
    [CS-DIST-p0221-s05] Then T is n-discerning if, there exist a state q0, teams A0 and A1, and operations π1, . . . , πn, such that RA0,j ∩RA1,j = ∅for all j.
    [CS-DIST-p0223-s29] Theorem 19.3.4.
    [CS-DIST-p0223-s30] For any readable object T, hrm(T) ≥n if and only if T is n-discerning.
- CS-DIST-C03-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Registers, and objects whose operations are only reads plus non-returning read-modify-write (modify-write) operations that are interfering (any two either commute or one overwrites the other), have consensus number 1, because an FLP-style argument shows that no pair of operations can leave a bivalent configuration for a univalent one.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s14] There’s a pattern to these cases that generalizes to other objects.
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s15] Suppose that an object has a read operation that returns its state and one or more read-modify-write operations that don’t return anything (perhaps we could call them “modify-write” operations).
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s16] We’ll say that the MW operations are interfering if, for any two operations x and y, either:
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s17] • x and y commute: Cxy = Cyx.
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s18] • One of x and y overwrites the other: Cxy = Cy or Cyx = Cx.
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s19] Then no pair of read or modify-write operations can get us out of a bivalent state, because (a) reads commute; (b) for a read and MW, the non-reader can’t tell which operation happened ﬁrst; (c) and for any two MW operations, either they commute or the overwriter can’t detect that the ﬁrst operation happened.
    [CS-DIST-p0211-s20] So any MW object with uninformative, interfering MW operations has consensus number 1.
- CS-DIST-C03-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: A non-trivial RMW object that returns the old value solves 2-process consensus when initialized to a value v with f(v) ≠ v: each process writes its input to a register, then applies the RMW operation, the first process sees v and decides its own value, and the second sees f(v) and decides the first process's value.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s07] Suppose now that we have a RMW object that returns the old value, and suppose that it is non-trivial in the sense that it has at least one RMW operation where the embedded function f that determines the new value is not the identity (otherwise RMW is just read).
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s08] Then there is some value v such that f(v)̸ = v.
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s09] To solve two-process consensus, have each process pi ﬁrst write its preferred value to a register ri, then execute the non-trivial RMW operation on the RMW object initialized to v.
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s10] The ﬁrst process to execute its operation sees v and decides its own value.
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s11] The second process sees f(v) and decides the ﬁrst process’s value (which it reads from the register).5 It follows that a non-trivial RMW object has consensus number at least 2.
- CS-DIST-C03-S2-04 | S2
  ATOM: A non-trivial read-modify-write object that returns the old value solves two-process consensus: each process writes its preferred value to a register, then applies the non-trivial operation to the object initialized to a value v with f(v) ≠ v; the first process sees v and decides its own value, and the second sees f(v) and decides the first process's value.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s07] Suppose now that we have a RMW object that returns the old value, and suppose that it is non-trivial in the sense that it has at least one RMW operation where the embedded function f that determines the new value is not the identity (otherwise RMW is just read).
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s08] Then there is some value v such that f(v)̸ = v.
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s09] To solve two-process consensus, have each process pi ﬁrst write its preferred value to a register ri, then execute the non-trivial RMW operation on the RMW object initialized to v.
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s10] The ﬁrst process to execute its operation sees v and decides its own value.
    [CS-DIST-p0212-s11] The second process sees f(v) and decides the ﬁrst process’s value (which it reads from the register).5 It follows that a non-trivial RMW object has consensus number at least 2.
- CS-DIST-C03-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Consensus numbers give only a partial picture of relative object strength: an object type with consensus number m cannot necessarily implement every object with consensus number m or lower in systems with more than m processes, as shown by an infinite family of objects $O_{m,k}$ all of consensus number m, where $O_{m,k}$ can implement $O_{m,k'}$ iff $k'\le k$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0206-s04] The converse claim, that objects with the same or higher consensus numbers can simulate those with lower ones, is not necessarily true: even though a type T with consensus number m can implement any object for n ≤m processes (see §19.4), in a system with n > m processes there may be objects with consensus number m that T can’t implement.
    [CS-DIST-p0206-s05] In particular, a result of Afek, Ellen, and Gafni [AEG16] gives an inﬁnitely family of objects Om,k for all m, k ≥2 with the property that every object Om,k has consensus number m, but Om,k can implement Om,k′ in a system with enough processes if and only if k′ ≤k.
    [CS-DIST-p0206-s06] So consensus numbers give only a partial picture of the relative strengths of diﬀerent objects.
- CS-DIST-C03-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Whether the $h^r_m$ hierarchy is robust for arbitrary deterministic objects is still open, though it is known to be robust for RMW registers and objects with a read operation that returns the current state, and for deterministic objects that do not discriminate between processes.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0207-s06] Whether or not the resulting hierarchy is in fact robust for arbitrary de- terministic objects is still open, but Ruppert [Rup00] subsequently showed that it is robust for RMW registers and objects with a read operation that returns the current state, and there is a paper by Borowsky, Gafni, and Afek [BGA94] that sketches a proof based on a topological characterization of computability3 that hrm is robust for deterministic objects that don’t discriminate between processes (unlike, say, single-writer registers).
